newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Lower rates help investment, hurt small banks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lower rates help investment, hurt small banks.

text.p: Russian banks used to making fat profits on low-risk government bonds are being forced to become an engine for the economy as yields fall and have to open credit lines to industry, bankers say.
But many smaller banks which relied on profits from state securities operations as their only source of funds will fall victims of the government's efforts to make the economy work.

"Previously banks were eager to lend to the government at high profitablity and the lowest possible risk in this country," Bank Menatep Treasury Head Nikolai Kuznetsov told Reuters. "A cut in the rates changes the orientation of the banking system."
Many Russian banks are heavily undercapitalised and were set up only to speculate on the government paper market. Even bigger banks hold a big part of their assets in government paper.
Annual yields on GKO discount Treasury bills have fallen to about 20 percent from about 200 percent a year ago and the central bank says the fall will continue to the end of the year.
LOWER RATES OPEN DOORS TO CHEAPER FOREIGN FUNDS...
Successful banks may compensate losses from lower yields and credit rates by increasing the volume of operations.

An international credit rating recently received by Russia, and lower rates as part of general stabilisation of the economy, were opening doors for Russian banks to get ratings and access cheaper foreign funds, Kuznetsov said.
The local banks, which have been reluctant to take advantage of foreign credit lines fearing default from local companies, are likely to increase their lending activity as well, he said.
"The rate cut produces a double effect -- banks could unfreeze foreign banks' credit lines and get funds under sensible interest rates abroad," he said.
The State Statistics Committee said the year through May 1997 was the first time since economic reforms began that investment in the industrial sector did not shrink.
...BUT MAY BE DEATH KNELL FOR SMALLER BANKS
But bankers said lower profits from T-bill operations would kill small and medium-sized banks, portfolios, which consisted mainly of government securities.
"It will speed up the process of diminishing the number of banking institutions," Tokobank Executive Vice-President Pavel Nefidov said. "Small regional banks will be first to go."

Association of Russian Banks Executive Vice President Vyacheslav Zakharov said banks' total profit in the first quarter of 1997 fell two-fold compared to a year earlier, mainly due to the fall in T-bill yields.
"Banks no longer have a stable and high profit," he said.
The central bank has also lowered its refinancing rate, effectively a tax on T-bill yields, to 24 percent from 36 percent as of June 16.
But the move also will require depositors to pay taxes on funds in accounts at interest rates higher than the new rate.
Average deposit rates at banks are now between 28 and 30 percent, while credit rates are around 45 percent.
"Banking business will concenrate in big banking groups, while smaller banks will either have serious financial difficulties or will have to merge," Kuznetsov said.
Some banks unable to manage new changes will collapse as well, said Mosbusinessbank Analysis Department Head Georgy Sychyov.
He said banks were wary of providing credits to industry, above all because the economy suffered from a severe non-payment crisis.
Non-payments between industrial enterprises reached 1,000 trillion roubles ($173 billion) in the first four months of 1997, while the gross domestic product was 810 trillion roubles.
"The number of banks will shrink in proportion with the fall in T-bill yields," he said. ($ = 5788 Russian Roubles)
